_comment: Centralized definitions - Single source of truth for all topics

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Think of {term:loss:loss} as a 'wrongness score'. Like a teacher grading a test - 0 means perfect, higher means more mistakes. The {term:model:model}'s goal is to get this as close to 0 as possible.

Cross-entropy {term:loss:loss} measures the negative log-likelihood of the correct {term:token:token}. Lower values indicate the {term:model:model} assigns higher {term:probability:probability} to correct answers.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The capital of France is ___'

Step 1: {term:model:Model} outputs {term:probability:probabilities} for all {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} entries
Step 2: {term:model:Model} assigns probabilities:
{"Paris": 0.90, "Lyon": 0.03, "Berlin": 0.02, ...49997 others} Step 3: Correct answer is 'Paris', so:
{term:loss:L} = −log(0.90) ≈ 0.105 Step 4: Low {term:loss:loss}! {term:model:Model} was confident and correct.

Bad case (low confidence):
{"Paris": 0.10, "Lyon": 0.08, "Berlin": 0.07, ...} {term:loss:L} = −log(0.10) ≈ 2.3 (HIGH = needs improvement!)

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
Training objective: Minimize average {term:loss:loss} across all {term:token:tokens} in the training {term:data:corpus}.

Typical values:
• Pre-trained LLM: {term:loss:L} ≈ 2-3 (perplexity ~8-20)
• After fine-tuning: {term:loss:L} ≈ 1.5-2.5
• On memorized text: {term:loss:L} → 0

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Imagine you're blindfolded on a hill trying to reach the bottom (lowest {term:loss:loss}). The {term:gradient:gradient} tells you which direction is steepest downhill. It's your 'compass' for improving the {term:model:model}.

{term:gradient:∇}{term:loss:L} is a vector of partial derivatives of the {term:loss:loss} function with respect to each {term:weights:weight} parameter. It points in the direction of steepest increase, so we move opposite to it.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: Current {term:weights:weights} θ = [2.0, 3.0, 1.5]
Step 2: Compute {term:loss:loss} on a batch of {term:data:data}
Step 3: Calculate {term:gradient:gradient}: {term:gradient:∇}L = [0.1, -0.2, 0.05]
Step 4: Apply learning rate (lr = 0.001):
θ_new = θ − lr × {term:gradient:∇}L
θ_new = [2.0, 3.0, 1.5] − [0.0001, -0.0002, 0.00005]
Step 5: New {term:weights:weights} = [1.9999, 3.0002, 1.49995]
Result: {term:loss:Loss} should be slightly lower now!

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
What the gradient looks like:
For LLaMA-7B, {term:gradient:∇L} has the same shape as {term:weights:θ}: 7 billion numbers!

# Gradient for one attention layer (simplified) ∇W_Q = [[0.001, -0.003, ...], # 4096 × 4096 matrix [0.002, 0.001, ...], ...] Gradient accumulation: With large {term:model:models}, we often can't fit the full batch in memory. We accumulate {term:gradient:gradients} over multiple mini-batches before applying the update.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The 'brain' of the {term:model:model} - all the learned numbers that determine how it responds. Different {term:weights:θ} = different {term:model:model}.
The set of all learnable parameters in a neural network. For LLMs, this includes embeddings, attention {term:weights:weights} (Q, K, V projections), FFN {term:weights:weights}, and layer norms.
sections.formula: {term:weights:θ} ∈ ℝⁿ where n = number of parameters

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:weights:θ} represents billions of parameters: embedding matrices, attention weights, MLP weights. For GPT-4: ~1.7T {term:weights:parameters}. For LLaMA-7B: 7 billion {term:weights:parameters}.

sections.title: What Weights Look Like
sections.content:
A single Linear layer (768 → 768):
W = [[ 0.023, -0.015, 0.087, ...], # 768 columns [ 0.042, 0.156, -0.034, ...], [-0.008, 0.091, 0.023, ...], ... # 768 rows ] # Shape: (768, 768) = 589,824 params LLaMA-7B composition:
• Token embeddings: 32,000 × 4,096 = 131M params
• Each of 32 layers: ~218M params
• Total: ~7 billion {term:weights:parameters} stored in ~14GB (FP16)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Training {term:data:data} is the 'textbooks' the {term:model:model} learns from. Just like a student studying - better books lead to better knowledge. Garbage in = garbage out.

{term:data:D} = {x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ} is the corpus of text sequences. Each xᵢ is tokenized into {term:token:tokens}. The {term:model:model} learns the statistical distribution P(xᵢ) to minimize {term:loss:loss} over {term:data:D}.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:data:D} is the pretraining corpus: web pages (Common Crawl), books, Wikipedia, GitHub code, etc. For GPT-3: ~300B {term:token:tokens} (weighted training mix). The coverage and quality of {term:data:D} determines what the {term:model:model} 'knows'.

sections.title: What Training Data Looks Like
sections.content:
Pre-training data (next token prediction):
Batch of 4 sequences, each 512 tokens: [ [15496, 11, 995, 0, ...], # "Hello, world!..." [464, 3139, 286, 4881, ...], # "The capital of France..." [1212, 318, 257, 1332, ...], # "This is a test..." [8496, 284, 262, 6908, ...], # "Welcome to the future..." ] Shape: (batch_size=4, seq_len=512) SFT data (instruction-following):
{ "instruction": "Explain quantum physics simply", "input": "", "output": "Imagine tiny particles that can be in..." } RLHF data (preference pairs):
{ "prompt": "What's the weather?", "chosen": "I don't have access to real-time data...", "rejected": "It's sunny today!" # Hallucination! }

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: A {term:token:token} is a chunk of text that the {term:model:model} actually 'sees'. Words get broken into pieces that exist in the {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}. The {term:model:model} doesn't work with text directly - it works with numeric IDs!

{term:token:Tokens} are produced by a tokenizer (BPE, SentencePiece, WordPiece). Each {term:token:token} maps to an integer ID in range [0, {term:vocabulary:vocab_size}). The {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} is fixed during training, typically 32K-100K entries.

sections.title: Visual Example: Word → Token → ID
sections.content:
Input text: 'Hello, world!'

Step 1 - Tokenization:
'Hello' → ['Hello'] → [{term:token:15496}]
',' → [','] → [{term:token:11}]
' world' → [' world'] → [{term:token:995}]
'!' → ['!'] → [{term:token:0}]

Step 2 - What {term:model:model} sees:
[15496, 11, 995, 0] ← Just numbers!

Subword example:
'Unbelievable' → ['Un', 'believ', 'able'] → [{term:token:1525}, {term:token:6975}, {term:token:540}]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: A {term:probability:probability distribution} is the {term:model:model}'s 'confidence spread' over ALL possible next {term:token:tokens}. Think of it as betting chips - the {term:model:model} distributes 100% across every word in the {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}. Higher % = more confident that's the next word.

{term:probability:P}({term:token:t}|context) = {term:softmax:softmax}({term:logits:logits})[{term:token:t}]. The {term:model:model} outputs raw {term:logits:logits} (one per {term:vocabulary:vocab} entry), then {term:softmax:softmax} converts them to a valid {term:probability:probability} distribution that sums to 1.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The capital of France is'

Step 1: {term:model:Model} outputs {term:logits:logits} for all 50K {term:vocabulary:vocab} entries
Step 2: Apply {term:softmax:softmax} to convert to {term:probability:probabilities}
Step 3: Result (showing top tokens):
{ "Paris": 0.92, "Lyon": 0.03, "Berlin": 0.01, "Rome": 0.005, ...49,996 others share 0.035 } Key property: {term:summation:Σ} of ALL {term:probability:probabilities} = 1.0 (always!)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Think of {term:reward:reward} as a 'quality score' or 'star rating' for responses. Like rating restaurant reviews - 5 stars for helpful, accurate answers; 1 star for unhelpful or wrong ones. The {term:model:model} learns to get more stars!

A scalar function trained on human preference {term:data:data}. Given pairs (response_A, response_B) where humans prefer A, the {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model} learns to assign higher scores to preferred responses. Training uses Bradley-Terry model with cross-entropy {term:loss:loss}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: User asks: 'Explain gravity to a 5-year-old'
Step 2: {term:model:Model} generates two responses:
• Response A: 'Gravity is like invisible glue that pulls things down...'
• Response B: 'Gravity is the curvature of spacetime caused by mass...'
Step 3: {term:reward:Reward} {term:model:model} scores both:
• {term:reward:R}(A) = 0.85 (appropriate for audience)
• {term:reward:R}(B) = 0.32 (too complex)
Step 4: {term:model:Model} {term:policy:policy} is updated via {term:gradient:gradients} to generate more A-like responses
Result: {term:model:Model} learns to tailor responses to the audience!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:policy:policy} IS the LLM - it's the 'decision maker'. Like a chef deciding what ingredients to add next, the {term:policy:policy} decides what {term:token:token} to generate next. It's the {term:model:model}'s 'personality' or 'strategy' for responding.

A {term:policy:policy} maps prompts to {term:probability:probability} distributions over responses. In LLMs, it's the full {term:model:model} with {term:weights:weights} {term:weights:θ}. Each response's {term:probability:probability} is the product of {term:token:token} {term:probability:probabilities}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: User says 'Hi'
Step 2: {term:policy:Policy π} considers possible responses:
• 'Hello!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.05
• 'Hi there!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.12
• 'Hey!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.08
Step 3: During RLHF, we discover 'Hi there!' gets higher {term:reward:reward}
Step 4: Update {term:weights:θ} via {term:gradient:gradient} to increase {term:probability:P}('Hi there!')
Step 5: After training, new {term:policy:policy} might give:
• 'Hi there!' → {term:probability:P} = 0.25 (increased!)
Result: {term:policy:Policy} now favors higher-{term:reward:reward} responses!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:value:value} function is like a 'fortune teller' for {term:reward:rewards}. Given where we are in generating a response, it predicts: 'How good will the final response probably be?' It helps the {term:model:model} know if it's on the right track mid-generation.
The {term:expectation:expected} cumulative {term:reward:reward} from a given state. In RLHF, a 'critic' network estimates {term:value:V} to compute {term:advantage:advantages}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: {term:model:Model} is mid-response: 'The answer is...'
Step 2: {term:value:Value} function predicts: 'Based on this start, {term:expectation:expected} final {term:reward:reward} ≈ 0.6'
Step 3: {term:model:Model} completes: 'The answer is 42'
Step 4: Actual {term:reward:reward} = 0.8
Step 5: {term:advantage:Advantage} = 0.8 - 0.6 = +0.2 (better than {term:expectation:expected}!)
Step 6: This positive {term:advantage:advantage} encourages similar responses

Note: GRPO eliminates the {term:value:value} function by using group statistics instead!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: {term:kl:KL divergence} measures 'how different' two {term:probability:probability} distributions are. Think of it as a 'drift detector' - it alerts us when the RL-trained {term:model:model} strays too far from the original SFT {term:model:model}. It's like keeping a student on track so they don't learn bad habits while trying to get good grades.

Measures how one {term:probability:probability} distribution differs from another. Properties: Always ≥ 0, equals 0 iff P = Q, asymmetric (KL(P||Q) ≠ KL(Q||P)). In RLHF, penalizes deviation from the SFT baseline.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
Scenario: Reference model (SFT) vs RL policy responding to 'How are you?'

Token probabilities for 4 response options:
SFT (π_ref) RL (π) 'I'm good' 0.4 0.1 'Fine' 0.3 0.05 'Great!' 0.2 0.05 'AMAZING!!' 0.1 0.8 ← RL loves this! KL divergence calculation:
KL(π || π_ref) = Σ π(x) × log(π(x) / π_ref(x)) = 0.1×log(0.1/0.4) + 0.05×log(0.05/0.3) + 0.05×log(0.05/0.2) + 0.8×log(0.8/0.1) = 0.1×(-1.39) + 0.05×(-1.79) + 0.05×(-1.39) + 0.8×(2.08) = -0.14 + -0.09 + -0.07 + 1.66 ≈ 1.36 bits ← HIGH! RL drifted too far Result: High KL → apply penalty to prevent reward hacking!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:advantage:advantage} tells you how much BETTER (or worse) a specific action is compared to what you'd typically expect from that situation. Think of it like a student's performance: if the class average is 70% and you scored 85%, your {term:advantage:advantage} is +15 points. In RL, we want to reinforce actions with positive {term:advantage:advantage} (better than usual) and discourage actions with negative {term:advantage:advantage} (worse than usual).

{term:advantage:A}(s,a) = Q(s,a) − {term:value:V}(s), where Q(s,a) is the action-value (expected return from taking action a in state s), and {term:value:V}(s) is the baseline (expected return from state s under the current {term:policy:policy}). In GRPO, we use group statistics: {term:advantage:A}_i = ({term:reward:R}_i − mean({term:reward:R})) / std({term:reward:R}).

sections.title: In LLMs (RLHF)
sections.content: During RLHF, for each generated response, we compute its {term:advantage:advantage} relative to the {term:value:value function}'s prediction. Responses with positive {term:advantage:advantage} (scored higher than expected by the {term:reward:reward} model) are reinforced; negative {term:advantage:advantage} responses are discouraged.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation (GRPO)
sections.content:
Prompt: 'Explain photosynthesis simply'

Step 1 - Generate 4 responses and get rewards:
rewards = [0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.3] Step 2 - Compute group statistics:
mean = (0.2 + 0.5 + 0.8 + 0.3) / 4 = 0.45 std = 0.23 Step 3 - Calculate normalized advantages:
A₁ = (0.2 - 0.45) / 0.23 = -1.09 ← Discourage! A₂ = (0.5 - 0.45) / 0.23 = +0.22 ← Slightly reinforce A₃ = (0.8 - 0.45) / 0.23 = +1.52 ← Strongly reinforce! A₄ = (0.3 - 0.45) / 0.23 = -0.65 ← Discourage Result: Response 3 (best in group) gets largest positive update!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:reference:reference} {term:policy:policy} is your 'safety copy' - the well-behaved SFT {term:model:model} frozen in time. It's like having a responsible adult supervising a teenager (the RL {term:policy:policy}) who's trying new things. Keeps the {term:model:model} from going off the rails.
A frozen copy of the {term:policy:policy} {term:weights:weights} from before RL training. The {term:kl:KL} penalty constrains how far the trained {term:policy:policy} can deviate from this baseline.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: Start with SFT {term:model:model} → Save copy as {term:reference:π_ref} (frozen)
Step 2: Initialize RL {term:policy:policy} {term:policy:π} = copy of SFT {term:model:model} (trainable)
Step 3: During RL, {term:model:model} learns responding 'ABSOLUTELY FANTASTIC!!!' gets high {term:reward:reward}
Step 4: But {term:reference:π_ref} would say 'I'm doing well, thank you'
Step 5: {term:kl:KL}({term:policy:π}||{term:reference:π_ref}) = HIGH (big difference)
Step 6: High {term:kl:KL} penalty reduces the objective, discouraging this
Result: {term:model:Model} improves but stays grounded in normal language!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} is the {term:model:model}'s complete dictionary - every word piece it knows. Think of it as a numbered list where each entry has an ID. If a word isn't in the {term:vocabulary:vocab}, it gets split into smaller pieces that ARE.

The fixed set of all {term:token:tokens} the {term:model:model} can recognize and generate. Each {term:token:token} maps to a unique integer ID. The {term:model:model} outputs {term:logits:logits} with shape [|{term:vocabulary:V}|].

sections.title: What Vocabulary Looks Like
sections.content:
Sample entries (GPT-style):
ID 0: '!'
ID 11: ','
ID 262: ' the'
ID 995: ' world'
ID 15496: 'Hello'

Size matters:
• GPT-2: 50,257 entries
• LLaMA: 32,000 entries
• GPT-4: ~100K entries

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: {term:softmax:Softmax} converts raw scores ({term:logits:logits}) into {term:probability:probabilities}. It's like converting test scores into percentages - bigger scores get bigger percentages, and they all add up to 100%.

{term:softmax:softmax}(z)_i = exp(z_i) / {term:summation:Σ}_j exp(z_j). Properties: (1) Output ∈ (0,1), (2) {term:summation:Σ} outputs = 1, (3) Preserves order of inputs, (4) Amplifies differences between values.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Step 1: {term:model:Model} outputs {term:logits:logits}: [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]
Step 2: Compute exp: [7.39, 2.72, 1.11]
Step 3: Sum: 7.39 + 2.72 + 1.11 = 11.22
Step 4: Divide each by sum:
• {term:probability:P}_0 = 7.39/11.22 = 0.66
• {term:probability:P}_1 = 2.72/11.22 = 0.24
• {term:probability:P}_2 = 1.11/11.22 = 0.10
Result: [0.66, 0.24, 0.10] - sums to 1.0!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: {term:logits:Logits} are the raw 'scores' the neural network produces before converting to {term:probability:probabilities}. They can be any number (positive, negative, huge). Think of them as the {term:model:model}'s 'pre-grades' before being curved.

Raw unnormalized scores from the final linear layer. Higher {term:logits:logit} = {term:model:model} more favors that {term:token:token}. Apply {term:softmax:softmax} to convert to {term:probability:probabilities}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The capital of France is'

Step 1: Text → {term:token:token} IDs → embeddings
Step 2: Pass through transformer layers
Step 3: Final layer outputs {term:logits:logits} for each {term:vocabulary:vocab} entry:
• 'Paris' (ID 6342): {term:logits:logit} = 4.2 (high!)
• 'London' (ID 4712): {term:logits:logit} = 1.1
• 'the' (ID 262): {term:logits:logit} = -2.3
Step 4: Apply {term:softmax:softmax} to get {term:probability:probabilities}

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:model:model} is the entire 'brain' - the neural network that takes {term:input:input} and produces {term:output:output}. It's the combination of architecture (how layers connect) + {term:weights:weights} (learned numbers). Same architecture + different {term:weights:weights} = different {term:model:model}.

A parameterized function mapping {term:input:inputs} to {term:output:outputs}. For LLMs: {term:input:input} = {term:token:token} sequence, {term:output:output} = {term:logits:logits} over {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}. Architecture defines the function class; training finds optimal {term:weights:θ}.

sections.title: What's Inside a Model
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B architecture:
• Embedding: {term:vocabulary:vocab} → 4096-dim vectors
• 32 transformer layers, each with:
- Self-attention (Q, K, V projections)
- MLP (feed-forward network)
- Layer normalization
• Final linear: 4096 → {term:vocabulary:vocab_size}

Total: 7 billion {term:weights:parameters} = the learned 'knowledge'

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:summation:Σ} symbol means 'add everything up'. When you see {term:summation:Σ}_i, it means 'for each value of i, compute what's inside, then add all results together'. It's shorthand for a loop that adds.

{term:summation:Σ}_{i=a}^{b} f(i) = f(a) + f(a+1) + ... + f(b). In {term:loss:loss} functions, we sum over all {term:token:tokens} in a sequence. In {term:softmax:softmax}, we sum over all {term:vocabulary:vocab} entries.

sections.title: Examples in LLM Training
sections.content:
In Cross-Entropy {term:loss:Loss}:
{term:loss:L} = -{term:summation:Σ}_{i=1}^{T} log P(t_i)
= -log P(t_1) - log P(t_2) - ... - log P(t_T)
Sum {term:loss:loss} over all T {term:token:tokens}

In {term:softmax:Softmax}:
{term:summation:Σ}_j exp(z_j) = exp(z_1) + exp(z_2) + ...
Sum over all {term:vocabulary:vocab} entries

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
{term:variance:Variance} measures 'spread' or 'disagreement'. Imagine asking 5 different {term:model:models} the same question:

• If they ALL say "Paris" with 92% confidence → Low {term:variance:variance} (agreement)
• If they say "Paris" (30%), "London" (25%), "Berlin" (20%)... → High {term:variance:variance} (disagreement)

High {term:variance:variance} = high uncertainty about the answer.
{term:variance:Var}({term:input:X}) = {term:expectation:E}[({term:input:X} - μ)²] - the {term:expectation:expected} squared deviation from the mean.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:variance:Variance} of what? {term:output:Token} {term:probability:probabilities}. If you sample 10 different {term:model:model} checkpoints and ask them to predict the next {term:token:token} after 'The capital of France is', {term:variance:variance} measures how much their {term:probability:probability} for 'Paris' differs (e.g., 0.82, 0.91, 0.76, 0.88...).

sections.title: In Classic ML
sections.content:
Random Forest: If 90/100 trees predict "spam", {term:variance:variance} across trees is low (confident). If 50/50 split, {term:variance:variance} is high.

Linear Regression: Confidence intervals come from prediction {term:variance:variance}. House price = $350K ± $15K means {term:variance:variance} captures uncertainty in the estimate.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
5 {term:model:models} predict {term:probability:P}('Paris'):
values = [0.82, 0.88, 0.79, 0.91, 0.85] Step 1: Calculate mean (μ):
μ = (0.82 + 0.88 + 0.79 + 0.91 + 0.85) / 5 = 0.85 Step 2: Calculate squared differences:
(0.82-0.85)² = 0.0009 (0.88-0.85)² = 0.0009 (0.79-0.85)² = 0.0036 (0.91-0.85)² = 0.0036 (0.85-0.85)² = 0.0000 Step 3: Average = {term:variance:Variance}:
Var = (0.0009 + 0.0009 + 0.0036 + 0.0036 + 0) / 5 = 0.0018 Result: Low {term:variance:variance} = {term:model:models} mostly agree!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The 'brain' of the {term:model:model} - all the learned {term:weights:weights} that determine how it responds. Different {term:theta:θ} = different {term:model:model}.
The set of all learnable parameters in a neural network. For LLMs, this includes embeddings, attention {term:weights:weights} (Q, K, V), FFN {term:weights:weights}, and layer norms.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:theta:θ} represents billions of parameters: embedding matrices, attention weights (Q, K, V projections), FFN weights, layer norms. For GPT-4: ~1.7T parameters. For LLaMA-7B: 7 billion parameters.

sections.title: In Classic ML
sections.content:
Linear Regression: {term:theta:θ} = weight coefficients (β₀, β₁, ..., βₙ). A house price {term:model:model} might have θ = [intercept, coef_sqft, coef_beds, coef_location].

Random Forest: {term:theta:θ} = all tree structures, split thresholds, and leaf values across all trees.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B has {term:theta:θ} with 7 billion floats stored in ~14GB (FP16).

{term:theta:θ} includes:
• {term:token:Token} embeddings: [vocab_size × hidden_dim]
• 32 transformer layers, each with attention + FFN {term:weights:weights}
• Final classification head

Different checkpoints (epoch 1 vs epoch 10) have different {term:theta:θ} values.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:output:output} is what the {term:model:model} produces - the answer, prediction, or generated content. Think of it as the 'answer sheet' that the {term:model:model} fills out based on the question ({term:input:input}). In classification, it's a category label. In regression, it's a number. In generation (like LLMs), it's a sequence of {term:token:tokens} - the actual text the model writes.

The target random variable {term:output:y} that the {term:model:model} aims to predict. All predictions are conditional: {term:probability:P}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}, {term:theta:θ}). In supervised learning (classification/regression), {term:output:y} is the label. In generative models, {term:output:y} is the generated sequence.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:output:y} is the next {term:token:token} (or full completion). Critically, it's not just a single word - it's a {term:probability:probability distribution} over the entire {term:vocabulary:vocabulary}. Shape: [vocab_size] ≈ [50,000+] {term:probability:probabilities} summing to 1. The actual {term:token:token} chosen depends on the decoding strategy (greedy, beam search, nucleus sampling, etc.).

sections.title: In Classic ML
sections.content:
Linear Regression: {term:output:y} = predicted house price ($350K)
Logistic Regression: {term:output:y} = class probability (88% spam)
Random Forest: {term:output:y} = majority vote across trees

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
{term:input:Prompt}: 'The capital of France is'

Step 1: {term:model:Model} processes {term:input:input}, outputs {term:logits:logits}
Step 2: Apply {term:softmax:softmax} to get {term:output:y} = distribution:
{Paris: 0.92, Lyon: 0.03, Berlin: 0.01, ...}
Step 3: Decoding picks 'Paris' (highest prob)
Step 4: This becomes context for next {term:output:y} prediction

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:input:input} is everything the {term:model:model} 'sees' before making its prediction - the question, context, prompt, or features. Think of it as the 'question paper' given to the student ({term:model:model}). The {term:model:model}'s job is to produce an {term:output:output} based ONLY on this {term:input:input}. In ML, we always write predictions as conditional: given {term:input:x}, predict {term:output:y}.

The conditioning variable for all predictions. Formally: {term:probability:P}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}, {term:theta:θ}). In supervised learning, {term:input:x} is the feature vector. In sequence models, {term:input:x} is the input sequence. All uncertainty, predictions, and {term:model:model} behavior are conditional on {term:input:x}.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:input:x} is the prompt + conversation history. It's tokenized into a sequence of {term:token:token} IDs → embedded into vectors → processed through transformer layers. The ENTIRE context window is the {term:input:input} at each generation step. Context length limits (4K, 32K, 128K) bound how much {term:input:x} the model can 'see'.

sections.title: In Classic ML
sections.content:
Linear Regression: {term:input:x} = [sqft, bedrooms, location] features
Logistic Regression: {term:input:x} = email text features (word counts, etc.)
Random Forest: {term:input:x} = tabular row of features

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
User types: 'Translate to French: Good morning'

Step 1 - Tokenization:
{term:input:x} = ['Trans', 'late', ' to', ' French', ':', ' Good', ' morning']
Step 2 - ID Conversion:
{term:input:x} = [45023, 378, 284, 4141, 25, 4599, 3329]
Step 3 - Embedding:
Each ID → 4096-dim vector
Step 4: {term:model:Model} predicts {term:output:y} conditioned on this {term:input:x}

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Before seeing any {term:data:data}, you have initial beliefs about what {term:theta:θ} might be (the prior). After observing {term:data:data}, you UPDATE your beliefs - this updated belief is the {term:posterior:posterior}. It's like a detective: before evidence, many suspects are plausible. After evidence, some become more/less likely. The {term:posterior:posterior} is a DISTRIBUTION, not a single value - it tells you the relative plausibility of ALL possible {term:theta:θ} values.

Bayes' Theorem: {term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D}) = [{term:posterior:p}({term:data:D}|{term:theta:θ}) × {term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ})] / {term:posterior:p}({term:data:D}). The posterior combines the likelihood (how well {term:theta:θ} explains the {term:data:data}) with the prior (initial beliefs). The denominator {term:posterior:p}({term:data:D}) is the marginal likelihood (normalizing constant).

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
Exact {term:posterior:posteriors} are intractable for LLMs (billions of {term:theta:parameters}). We approximate via:
• Ensembles: Train N {term:model:models}, each represents a 'sample' from {term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})
• MC Dropout: Different dropout masks ≈ different effective {term:theta:θ}
• Checkpoint Ensembles: Different training epochs = different {term:theta:θ} samples

sections.title: Step-by-Step Visual Example
sections.content:
Scenario: Estimating a coin's bias (θ = probability of heads)

Step 1 - Prior belief: Before flipping, assume fair coin
Prior: θ ~ Beta(1, 1) # Uniform - any value 0-1 equally likely Most likely θ = 0.5 Step 2 - Observe data: Flip 10 times → 8 heads, 2 tails
Data: D = {H, H, H, T, H, H, H, H, T, H} Step 3 - Compute posterior:
Posterior: θ|D ~ Beta(1+8, 1+2) = Beta(9, 3) Most likely θ = 9/(9+3) = 0.75 Result: Data shifted our belief from 0.5 → 0.75, with reduced uncertainty!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
The {term:expectation:expected value} is the 'weighted average' – what you'd get on average if you repeated an experiment many times.

Think of it as: If a coin gives $10 on heads (50%) and $0 on tails (50%), the {term:expectation:expected value} is $5 – not because you ever get $5, but because that's the long-run average.

In ML, we use {term:expectation:E} to average over uncertainty: 'What's the average {term:output:prediction} across all possible {term:model:models}?'
{term:expectation:E}[{term:input:X}] = ∫ {term:input:x}·{term:probability:p}({term:input:x})dx for continuous, or Σ {term:input:xᵢ}·{term:probability:p}({term:input:xᵢ}) for discrete.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
{term:expectation:E} is used as: 'average over {term:model:models}'.

{term:expectation:E}[{term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})][something] means: take many {term:model:model} samples (different {term:theta:θ}), compute 'something' for each, then average.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
5 {term:model:models} predict {term:probability:P}('Paris') as: [0.82, 0.88, 0.79, 0.91, 0.85]

{term:expectation:E}[{term:probability:P}('Paris')] = (0.82+0.88+0.79+0.91+0.85)/5 = 0.85

This is the 'consensus' {term:probability:probability} across {term:model:models}.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: How 'spread out' a {term:probability:probability distribution} is. Sharp peak = low {term:entropy:entropy} (confident). Flat distribution = high {term:entropy:entropy} (uncertain).
{term:entropy:H}({term:probability:p}) = −Σ {term:probability:p}({term:input:x})·log {term:probability:p}({term:input:x}). Measures {term:expectation:expected} surprise/information content.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
{term:entropy:H} measures {term:token:token}-level confidence. For each next-{term:token:token} prediction, compute {term:entropy:H} over the {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} distribution.

Range: 0 (one {term:token:token} has prob 1) to log(vocab_size) ≈ 15 bits (uniform over 50k {term:token:tokens}).

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The capital of France is'

Model output distribution (top tokens):
P = {"Paris": 0.95, "Lyon": 0.03, "Berlin": 0.02} Entropy calculation:
H = -[0.95×log₂(0.95) + 0.03×log₂(0.03) + 0.02×log₂(0.02)] H = -[0.95×(-0.074) + 0.03×(-5.06) + 0.02×(-5.64)] H = -[-0.07 + -0.15 + -0.11] H ≈ 0.33 bits ← Very confident! Compare to uncertain prompt: 'I feel ___'
P = {"good": 0.15, "bad": 0.12, "happy": 0.10, "sad": 0.08, ...} H ≈ 4.2 bits ← Much more uncertain!
{term:variance:Var}<sub>{term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})</sub>[{term:expectation:E}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}, {term:theta:θ})]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
How much do different {term:model:model} versions disagree on what the average answer should be?

Think of asking 5 different GPT checkpoints: "What's the capital of Atlantis?" If they each give a different confident answer, that disagreement is {term:epistemic-var:epistemic} uncertainty - the {term:model:models} don't have reliable knowledge.

The {term:variance:variance} computed across the {term:posterior:posterior distribution} over {term:theta:model parameters θ}, of the {term:expectation:expected value} of {term:output:output y} given {term:input:input x} and a specific {term:theta:θ}.

Key property: Reducible - can be decreased with more {term:data:training data}, better architecture, or RAG.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
Prompt: 'What is the capital of Narnia?'

5 model checkpoints predict P('Cair Paravel'):
Model 1: P = 0.75 (confident it's 'Cair Paravel') Model 2: P = 0.12 (thinks it's something else) Model 3: P = 0.65 Model 4: P = 0.08 (very uncertain) Model 5: P = 0.55 Step 1: Compute each model's mean prediction = [0.75, 0.12, 0.65, 0.08, 0.55]
Step 2: Take variance of these means:
μ = 0.43 Epistemic Var = Var([0.75, 0.12, 0.65, 0.08, 0.55]) = 0.076 Result: HIGH epistemic uncertainty! Models disagree → knowledge gap (fictional place).
{term:expectation:E}<sub>{term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})</sub>[{term:variance:Var}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}, {term:theta:θ})]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
How spread-out is each {term:model:model}'s own prediction, on average?

Think of the prompt: "Tell me a joke." Even a perfect {term:model:model} would have a flat {term:token:token} distribution - thousands of valid jokes exist! This internal spread is unavoidable because the {term:input:task itself} is ambiguous, not because the {term:model:model} lacks knowledge.

The {term:expectation:expected value} (average) computed across the {term:posterior:posterior distribution} over {term:theta:model parameters θ}, of the {term:variance:variance} of {term:output:output y} given {term:input:input x} and that specific {term:theta:θ}.

Key property: Irreducible - cannot be decreased even with infinite {term:data:data} or a perfect {term:model:model}. It's intrinsic to the task.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
Prompt: 'Tell me a joke about ___'

Each model's internal variance (spread in token probs):
Model 1: Variance of P(tokens) = 2.8 (many tokens equally valid) Model 2: Variance of P(tokens) = 2.5 Model 3: Variance of P(tokens) = 2.7 Model 4: Variance of P(tokens) = 2.9 Model 5: Variance of P(tokens) = 2.6 Step 1: List each model's internal variance: [2.8, 2.5, 2.7, 2.9, 2.6]
Step 2: Take AVERAGE of these variances:
Aleatoric Var = E[Var] = (2.8+2.5+2.7+2.9+2.6)/5 = 2.7 Result: HIGH aleatoric! Task is inherently ambiguous (many valid jokes).

sections.title: Intuition
sections.content: The complete 'I don't know' of the {term:model:model}. Combines both 'I lack knowledge' ({term:epistemic-var:epistemic}) and 'The task is ambiguous' ({term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric}).

sections.title: The Decomposition
sections.content:
{term:total-uncertainty:Total} = {term:epistemic-var:Epistemic} + {term:aleatoric-var:Aleatoric}

This is the Law of Total {term:variance:Variance} / {term:entropy:entropy} decomposition. We can separate the sources of uncertainty.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
{term:total-uncertainty:Total uncertainty} in a {term:token:token} prediction comes from:
• The {term:model:model} not knowing the answer ({term:epistemic-var:epistemic})
• Multiple {term:token:tokens} being valid completions ({term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric})

Uncertainty quantification helps us separate these to take appropriate action.

sections.title: Decomposition Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'What is the melting point of unobtainium?'

Total Uncertainty: HIGH

Breakdown (Variance form):
Total Var = 2.5 Epistemic (model disagreement) = 2.3 → Models give different answers: "1200°C", "800°C", "fictional" → REDUCIBLE: Could improve with better training data Aleatoric (inherent ambiguity) = 0.2 → Even within each model, slight uncertainty → IRREDUCIBLE: Multiple valid phrasings exist Compare to: 'Write a haiku about spring'
Total Var = 2.8 Epistemic = 0.3 # Models agree on haiku structure Aleatoric = 2.5 # Many valid haikus exist (irreducible!)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: {term:mutual-info:Mutual Information} measures how much knowing one variable tells you about another. If knowing X completely determines Y, {term:mutual-info:I}(X;Y) is high. If X and Y are independent (knowing one tells you nothing about the other), {term:mutual-info:I}(X;Y) = 0. Think of it as: 'How much does knowing the {term:input:input} reduce my uncertainty about the {term:output:output}?'

{term:mutual-info:I}(X;Y) = {term:entropy:H}(Y) − {term:entropy:H}(Y|X) = {term:entropy:H}(X) − {term:entropy:H}(X|Y). It's the reduction in {term:entropy:entropy} of one variable given knowledge of the other. Properties: Always non-negative, symmetric ({term:mutual-info:I}(X;Y) = {term:mutual-info:I}(Y;X)), measured in bits.

sections.title: In Uncertainty Quantification
sections.content: {term:mutual-info:Mutual Information} is used to decompose total uncertainty into {term:epistemic-info:epistemic} and {term:aleatoric-info:aleatoric} components (entropy version). {term:mutual-info:I}({term:output:y}; {term:theta:θ} | {term:input:x}, {term:data:D}) measures how much the {term:model:model} {term:theta:parameters θ} inform the prediction - this IS the {term:epistemic-info:epistemic uncertainty}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
Scenario: How much does knowing the prompt reduce output uncertainty?

Without prompt:
H(next_token) = log₂(50,000) ≈ 15.6 bits # Any token in vocab equally likely With prompt 'The capital of France is':
H(next_token | prompt) ≈ 0.5 bits # Almost certainly "Paris" Mutual Information:
I(next_token; prompt) = H(next_token) - H(next_token | prompt) = 15.6 - 0.5 = 15.1 bits Result: Knowing the prompt provides 15.1 bits of information about the next token!
{term:mutual-info:I}({term:output:y}, {term:theta:θ} | {term:input:x}, {term:data:D})

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
How much would knowing the "true" {term:model:model} reduce our uncertainty about the {term:output:output}?

If different {term:theta:model versions} give confidently different answers, that's high {term:mutual-info:mutual information}. Model A says "Paris" (99% confident), Model B says "London" (99% confident). They disagree - so the answer heavily depends on which {term:theta:θ} you ask.

The {term:mutual-info:mutual information} between {term:output:output y} and {term:theta:model parameters θ}, conditioned on {term:input:input x} and {term:data:training data D}.

Computed as: {term:entropy:H}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x},{term:data:D}) − {term:expectation:E}[{term:entropy:H}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x},{term:theta:θ})]

Key property: Reducible - measures knowledge gap that can be closed with more {term:data:data}.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
Prompt: 'Who won the 2024 US election?'

3 model checkpoints (trained at different times):
Model A (early 2024): H = 0.1 bits, answers "Unknown" Model B (late 2024): H = 0.2 bits, answers "Trump" Model C (mid 2024): H = 0.3 bits, answers "Biden" Key observation: Each model is internally CONFIDENT (low H)
BUT they DISAGREE with each other!

Compute Mutual Information (= Epistemic):
I(y; θ | x, D) = H(y|x,D) - E[H(y|x,θ)] ≈ Total entropy - Avg individual entropy = HIGH (because model disagree) Result: Knowing WHICH model would resolve uncertainty → epistemic!
{term:expectation:E}<sub>{term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})</sub>[{term:entropy:H}({term:posterior:p}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}, {term:theta:θ}))]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
{term:expectation:On average}, how "fuzzy" is each {term:theta:model's} {term:output:token distribution}?

All {term:theta:models} might agree that multiple {term:output:tokens} are valid. For "The weather today is ___", every {term:theta:model} assigns high {term:entropy:entropy} because "sunny", "rainy", "nice" are all valid. This shared fuzziness is the inherent ambiguity of the {term:input:task}.

The {term:expectation:expected value} (average) computed across the {term:posterior:posterior distribution} over {term:theta:model parameters θ}, of the {term:entropy:entropy} of that {term:theta:model's} {term:posterior:probability distribution} over {term:output:output y}.

Key property: Irreducible - even with infinite {term:data:data}, this {term:entropy:entropy} remains because the {term:input:task itself} is ambiguous.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The weather today is ___'

Each model's entropy (internal fuzziness):
Model 1: H = 3.2 bits (sunny, rainy, cloudy all valid) Model 2: H = 3.0 bits Model 3: H = 3.4 bits Model 4: H = 3.1 bits Model 5: H = 3.3 bits Key observation: ALL models have HIGH internal entropy
They AGREE that the task is ambiguous!

Compute Expected Entropy (= Aleatoric):
E[H(y|x,θ)] = (3.2 + 3.0 + 3.4 + 3.1 + 3.3) / 5 = 3.2 bits Result: Even a perfect model can't reduce this → irreducible aleatoric!
